title: Robinson's tropinone (1917)
goal: One pot, three simple pieces, two Mannich reactions: how Robinson made the tropane skeleton of atropine and cocaine.

problemSets.title: Iminium formation
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A primary amine and a 1,4-dialdehyde close a pyrrolidine ring and leave a cyclic iminium ion.
problemSets.conceptCard:
*Tropinone* is the bicyclic ketone at the heart of the tropane alkaloids (atropine, cocaine). Willstätter made it in 1901 in many steps from cycloheptanone. In 1917 Robert Robinson made it in **one pot**, in water at room temperature, from three simple pieces:

- **succinaldehyde** (butanedial), a 1,4-dialdehyde
- **methylamine**
- **acetonedicarboxylic acid** (3-oxopentanedioic acid)

He found it by imagining the molecule cut at the bonds a Mannich reaction makes: an early piece of *retrosynthetic* thinking, and a guess at how plants might do it.

The first job is the electrophile. Methylamine adds to one aldehyde as in imine formation. Its nitrogen, now a secondary amine, adds to the **second aldehyde in the same molecule**, closing a five-membered ring. Losing water from one of the two OH groups, pushed by the nitrogen lone pair, gives a **cyclic iminium ion**. A tertiary nitrogen has no N–H to lose, so the iminium ion stays put as the electrophile.

setItems.whyThisOne: Warm-up: the same addition and loss of water with one ketone.
Two additions of one nitrogen, a ring closure, and the cyclic iminium ion.

problemSets.title: First Mannich
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The enol of acetonedicarboxylic acid attacks the cyclic iminium ion and makes the first C–C bond.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In the **Mannich reaction** an enol attacks an iminium ion. Iminium ions are much better electrophiles than aldehydes, so even the small amount of enol present in water reacts with them.

Robinson first tried **acetone** as the nucleophile and got little tropinone. **Acetonedicarboxylic acid** works far better: each CH₂ sits between the ketone and a CO₂H, so it is doubly activated and enolises much more readily. The CO₂H groups are *activating groups*, to be removed at the end.

- acid-catalysed enolisation: protonate the ketone oxygen, then water removes an α-proton
- the enol carbon attacks the iminium carbon; the nitrogen gets its lone pair back
- water removes the proton from the protonated ketone

The product still has an OH next to the nitrogen (a masked second iminium ion) and a second enolisable CH₂.

In the flask, near pH 7, the CO₂H groups are mostly ionised and much of the amine is protonated; the problems draw the reacting forms.

setItems.whyThisOne: Warm-up: the Mannich reaction with acetone and an open-chain iminium ion.
Enolise the doubly activated ketone, then attack the cyclic iminium ion.

problemSets.title: Second Mannich
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A second enol meets a second iminium ion inside the same molecule and closes the tropane bicycle.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Everything needed for a second Mannich reaction is now in **one molecule**:

- the ketone enolises again, this time towards the **other α-carbon**, the CH₂ still next to a CO₂H
- the ring OH is protonated and pushed out by the nitrogen lone pair, giving a **second iminium ion** on the other side of the nitrogen
- the enol carbon attacks it: an **intramolecular** Mannich reaction closes a six-membered ring

The product, tropinone-2,4-dicarboxylic acid, has the *8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane* (tropane) skeleton: a pyrrolidine and a piperidine sharing the nitrogen and two carbons.

**Stereochemistry** (explained, not yet checked by the app): the nitrogen can only bridge two carbons on the same face, so the bicycle closes cis, and tropinone is a single, symmetrical (meso) compound with no optical activity.

setItems.whyThisOne: A second enol, a second iminium ion, and the ring closure that builds the bicycle.

problemSets.title: Decarboxylation
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: β-Keto acids lose CO₂ on heating through a six-membered ring of atoms, giving an enol.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Robinson acidified the mixture with hydrochloric acid and heated it to remove the two activating groups.

A carboxylic acid with a C=O **β** to it loses CO₂ easily, in one concerted step through a **six-membered ring of atoms**:

- the ketone oxygen takes the acid proton
- the O–H bond becomes a C=O of CO₂
- the C–C bond to the carboxyl carbon becomes the C=C of an **enol**

The enol then turns back into the ketone: H₃O⁺ protonates it on carbon and water takes the proton off oxygen. Here it happens **twice**, once on each side.

Later, Schöpf ran the reaction in buffer near pH 7 ("physiological conditions") and raised the yield to around 90%. Plants make tropinone by a related route, through the N-methylpyrrolinium ion.

setItems.whyThisOne: Two decarboxylations and two ketonisations finish tropinone.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Robinson's synthesis, and its parent Mannich reaction, shuffled with their names hidden.
problemSets.conceptCard:
The reactions of this track in random order and without their names. For each one, ask:

- is this step making the electrophile (an iminium ion) or the nucleophile (an enol)?
- which proton moves, and through which acid or base?
- for a ring closure: which atoms are close enough, and what size of ring forms?
- what drives the last step?
